item.title: OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse
item.description:
OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman introduced Dots, a new AI agent designed to set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI. The announcement included direct critiques of Meta’s Muse, with OpenAI positioning its new assistant as a more secure and trustworthy alternative to its primary competitor.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI executives used the launch of Dots to highlight security concerns surrounding Meta’s Muse, which had previously launched as a safer alternative to the agent OpenClaw. While Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised Muse was built for privacy and security, the platform has faced scrutiny over data collection and vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s leadership, including Codex product lead Alexander Embiricos, stated the company is focused on providing the most secure assistant while avoiding the mistakes of rivals.

⚙️ Key details

AI Agent Developer Stated Privacy and Security Approach
Dots OpenAI Zero data retention policy options for enterprises and individual user-set rules.
Muse Meta User data stored in isolated Linux VMs with browser, CPU, memory, and storage.
OpenClaw (Not specified) Predecessor to Muse; described as less safe than subsequent alternatives.

🧩 Capabilities and Controls

OpenAI and Meta have implemented different strategies to manage user data and agent behavior:

  • OpenAI Dots: Users can exert individual control over the agent, such as setting rules to prevent it from making purchases over a specific dollar amount. Enterprise customers can access frameworks with stronger data controls and options to ensure no data is stored on OpenAI servers.
  • Meta Muse: The agent defaults to allowing Meta to train models on user input, though an opt-out is available. While the company plans to introduce cryptographic methods to prevent internal access to VM data, Meta currently retains access.

🚀 Availability

OpenAI has launched Dots with a focus on its high-end user base, currently making it available only on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers. In contrast, Meta’s Muse saw rapid adoption following its release, gaining 600,000 daily active users in the United States within weeks and topping App Store charts.

💡 Why it matters

The push for more private AI agents comes as labs try to convince users to share increasingly personal information. Despite Meta’s privacy promises for Muse, security researchers exposed a zero-day vulnerability, and reports indicated the agent created detailed profiles of users’ social networks and shared private data, such as physical addresses and private messages, as part of its intended functions. OpenAI’s strategy with Dots relies on one-upping these rivals by promising stricter data boundaries, though some users still report discomfort when asked to provide sensitive financial information to these agents.

#OpenAI #Dots #Meta #AIAgents #DataPrivacy

Source: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

item.title: OpenAI Launches Dots Agent Platform for Pro Users
item.description:
OpenAI Launches Dots Agent Platform for Pro Users

OpenAI announced its new agent platform, called Dots, earlier this week. Think of Dots as Codex, but for regular people. The platform is enterprise software that can also order your dinner. Dots have blobby, anthropomorphic avatars and customizable names.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI’s new agent platform, Dots, is full of cute little guys who can do your bidding. In the future, OpenAI says you’ll be able to have multiple Dots, but right now you get one.

🧩 How it works

The interface looks similar to Muse’s; you chat with the agent in one window and follow its work in another as it clicks around on a virtual machine.

  • Your Dot’s virtual machine can access apps like Blender and GIMP right off the bat.
  • You can also give it access to your own computer through the desktop ChatGPT app.
  • You can call your Dot if you need to work through things out loud.

⚙️ Key details

OpenAI says Dots “can do nearly anything” with its cloud computer and access to apps. Testing revealed several practical examples:

  • Ordering dinner: It almost got there, and even found a $100 promotional discount in my email that I had mass deleted, but got stuck at a “human check.”
  • Purchasing: There’s no slick Stripe integration like Muse has to save your credit card info and use a virtual card for checkout. Dot paused to let me enter the numbers into the virtual browser; I didn’t trust it well enough to punch in my checking account number.
  • Booking a tour: It couldn’t find the option for a free tour and entry at a coworking space, and instead offered to sign me up for a $35 day pass.
  • Logging in: It reported that it was unable to log in to my Ikea account because it got stuck in a looping security check.
  • Restricted access: Elsewhere on the internet, the neighborhood teriyaki spot wouldn’t allow Dot onto its ordering page.
  • Security issues: Something about Dot’s footprint seems to get it tripped up on security checks more often than Muse or Instinct. Dot offered a link to OpenAI’s page about websites blocking its cloud browser traffic as an explanation.
  • Positive experience: I really saw Dot come into its element when I gave it access to something fully within my control: my personal website. I hashed out the changes I wanted section by section over 10 minutes, walked away to do some dishes, and got a ping that the next iteration was ready for me to review. I had to give it a shocking number of permissions, but it worked.
Aspect Detail
What it is AI agent platform, enterprise software, can order dinner
Avatars Blobby, anthropomorphic, customizable names
Number per user Currently one; multiple planned for the future
Interface Chat window + follow-along virtual machine view
Pre-installed apps Blender, GIMP
Computer access Via desktop ChatGPT app; phone calls supported
Model comparison Like Codex, but for regular people

🚀 Availability

OpenAI is offering Dots first to users on its highest-tier accounts, including the $100-per-month Pro account.

💡 Why it matters

Dots represents a new type of AI agent that aims to automate a wide range of tasks—from ordering dinner and booking tours to editing websites—directly from a chat interface. While it shows promise in controlled environments, it currently faces practical hurdles with security checks, e-commerce integrations, and website restrictions that limit its real-world usefulness.

#OpenAI #Dots #AIagents #automation #virtualmachine #enterprise

Source: OpenAI’s Dot agent is enterprise software that can also order your dinner

item.title: Introduction of Dots powered by Astra and ChatGPT Space
item.description:
Introduction of Dots powered by Astra and ChatGPT Space

A new AI development called “Dots” has been introduced, functioning alongside a new environment called ChatGPT Space.

🔍 Overview

Dots are powered by Astra, which Sam described as “our most aligned model,” intended to allow users to trust their Dot with “as much responsibility as you are comfortable with.

⚙️ Key details

  • ChatGPT Space: A new environment featuring a Notion-style slash menu.
  • Integration: Dots can have access to tools including ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams.
  • Capabilities: Dots can use Codex on a laptop to build apps and launch them in the iPhone Simulator.
  • Specialization: “Specialist dots” are being developed for sectors such as finance and legal.

🚀 Availability

ChatGPT Pro and Enterprise customers have access to Dots today.

#Astra #ChatGPTSpace #AIAgents #Dots

Source: OpenAI DevDay 2026 live blog
